t: Count Ways to Group Overlapping Ranges — Connected Components of Intervals
o: Partition intervals into two labeled groups so overlapping intervals share a group. Overlap is transitive through chains, so each connected component of the overlap graph can independently go to group 1 or group 2, giving 2^(#components) ways. Example 1: one component → 2. Example 2: [1,3],[2,5],[4,8] chain into one component and [10,20] is another → 2^2 = 4. After sorting by start, components are maximal chains where each interval starts before the running maximum end; with n up to 1e5 we need the O(n log n) sweep rather than pairwise overlap checks.
k: Overlapping is transitive via chaining, so count connected components of the interval graph.
Answer = 2^components mod 1e9+7; a sweep tracking the running max end identifies components in one pass.

a.i: Sort by start. Maintain the furthest end seen in the current component; if the next interval starts beyond it, a new component begins. Each component doubles the answer.
s: Sweep, extending the running end with max(end); on gap (start > running end) increment component count.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates the linear sweep
a.sp: O(1) extra (ignoring sort) — running end and counter

w: Sorting is the whole trick; note touching endpoints ([1,3],[3,5]) counts as overlapping since integer 3 is shared. Pitfalls: forgetting the modpow (components up to 1e5 → huge powers), and using strict inequality for overlap. Follow-up: count ways to split into k groups (answer k^components), or count components covering a queried point.
